{{Short description|Mathematical technique used in data compression and analysis}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=June 2024}}
[[File:Jpeg2000 2-level wavelet transform-lichtenstein.png|thumb|300px|An example of the 2D [[discrete wavelet transform]] that is used in [[JPEG2000]]]]
{{broader|Wavelet}}
In [[mathematics]], a '''wavelet series''' is a representation of a [[square-integrable]] ([[real number|real]]- or [[complex number|complex]]-valued) [[function (mathematics)|function]] by a certain [[orthonormal]] [[series (mathematics)|series]] generated by a [[wavelet]]. This article provides a formal, mathematical definition of an '''orthonormal wavelet''' and of the '''integral wavelet transform'''.<ref>Meyer, Yves (1992), Wavelets and Operators, Cambridge, UK: Cambridge University Press, {{ISBN|0-521-42000-8}}</ref><ref>Chui, Charles K. (1992), An Introduction to Wavelets, San Diego, CA: Academic Press, {{ISBN|0-12-174584-8}}</ref><ref>Daubechies, Ingrid. (1992), Ten Lectures on Wavelets, SIAM, {{ISBN|978-0-89871-274-2}}</ref><ref>Akansu, Ali N.; Haddad, Richard A. (1992), Multiresolution Signal Decomposition: Transforms, Subbands, and Wavelets, Boston, MA: Academic Press, {{ISBN|978-0-12-047141-6}}</ref>

==Definition==
A function <math> \psi \,\in\, L^2(\mathbb{R})</math> is called an '''orthonormal wavelet''' if it can be used to define a [[Hilbert space#Orthonormal bases|Hilbert basis]], that is, a [[Orthonormal_basis#Orthonormal_system|complete orthonormal system]] for the [[Hilbert space]] of [[square-integrable function]]s on the real line.

The Hilbert basis is constructed as the family of functions <math> \{\psi_{jk}:\, j,\, k \,\in\, \Z\}</math> by means of [[Dyadic transformation|dyadic]] [[translation (geometry)|translation]]s and [[dilation (operator theory)|dilation]]s of <math> \psi\,</math>,
<math display="block">\psi_{jk}(x) = 2^\frac{j}{2} \psi\left(2^jx - k\right),</math>
for integers <math> j,\, k \,\in\, \mathbb{Z}</math>.

If, under the standard [[inner product]] on <math> L^2\left(\mathbb{R}\right)</math>,
<math display="block">\langle f, g\rangle = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x)\overline{g(x)}dx,</math>
this family is orthonormal, then it is an orthonormal system:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
 \langle\psi_{jk},\psi_{lm}\rangle &= \int_{-\infty}^\infty \psi_{jk}(x)\overline{\psi_{lm}(x)}dx, \\
                  &=\delta_{jl}\delta_{km},
\end{align}</math>
where <math> \delta_{jl}\,</math> is the [[Kronecker delta]].

Completeness is satisfied if every function <math> f \,\in\, L^2\left(\mathbb{R}\right)</math> may be expanded in the basis as
:<math>f(x) = \sum_{j, k=-\infty}^\infty c_{jk} \psi_{jk}(x)</math>

with convergence of the series understood to be [[norm (mathematics)#Properties|convergence in norm]]. Such a representation of <math>f</math> is known as a '''wavelet series'''. This implies that an orthonormal wavelet is [[dual wavelet|self-dual]].

The '''integral wavelet transform''' is the [[integral transform]] defined as
<math display="block">\left[W_\psi f\right](a, b) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{|a|}} \int_{-\infty}^\infty \overline{\psi\left(\frac{x-b}{a}\right)}f(x)dx\,</math>
The '''wavelet coefficients''' <math> c_{jk}</math> are then given by
<math display="block">c_{jk} = \left[W_\psi f\right]\left(2^{-j}, k2^{-j}\right)</math>

Here, <math> a = 2^{-j}</math> is called the '''binary dilation''' or '''dyadic dilation''', and <math> b = k2^{-j}</math> is the '''binary''' or '''dyadic position'''.

==Principle==
The fundamental idea of wavelet transforms is that the transformation should allow only changes in time extension, but not shape, imposing a restriction on choosing suitable basis functions. Changes in the time extension are expected to conform to the corresponding analysis frequency of the basis function. Based on the [[Uncertainty principle#Signal processing|uncertainty principle]] of signal processing,

:<math>\Delta t \Delta \omega \geq \frac{1}{2}</math>

where <math> t </math> represents time and <math> \omega </math> [[angular frequency]] (<math>\omega=2 \pi f </math>, where <math> f</math> is [[ordinary frequency]]).

The higher the required resolution in time, the lower the resolution in frequency has to be. The larger the extension of the analysis [[Window function|windows]] is chosen, the larger is the value of <math> \Delta t</math>.

[[File:Basis function with compression factor.jpg|right|430px]]

When <math> \Delta t </math> is large
# Bad time resolution
# Good frequency resolution
# Low frequency, large scaling factor

When <math> \Delta t </math> is small
# Good time resolution
# Bad frequency resolution
# High frequency, small scaling factor

In other words, the basis function <math> \psi </math> can be regarded as an impulse response of a system with which the function <math> x(t) </math> has been filtered. The transformed signal provides information about the time and the frequency. Therefore, wavelet-transformation contains information similar to the [[Short-time Fourier transform|short-time-Fourier-transformation]], but with additional special properties of the wavelets, which show up at the resolution in time at higher analysis frequencies of the basis function. The difference in time resolution at ascending frequencies for the [[Fourier transform]] and the wavelet transform is shown below. Note however, that the frequency resolution is decreasing for increasing frequencies while the temporal resolution increases. This consequence of the [[Fourier uncertainty principle]] is not correctly displayed in the Figure.

[[File:STFT and WT.jpg|center|500px]]

This shows that wavelet transformation is good in time resolution of high frequencies, while for slowly varying functions, the frequency resolution is remarkable.

Another example: The analysis of three superposed sinusoidal signals <math> y(t) \;=\; \sin(2 \pi f_0 t) \;+\; \sin(4 \pi f_0 t) \;+\; \sin(8 \pi f_0 t)</math> with STFT and wavelet-transformation.

[[File:Analysis of three superposed sinusoidal signals.jpg|center|500px]]

==Wavelet compression==
{{See also|Discrete wavelet transform}}
'''Wavelet compression''' is a form of [[data compression]] well suited for [[image compression]] (sometimes also [[video compression]] and [[audio compression (data)|audio compression]]). Notable implementations are [[JPEG 2000]], [[DjVu]] and [[ECW (file format)|ECW]] for still images, [[JPEG XS]], [[CineForm]], and the BBC's [[Dirac (codec)|Dirac]]. The goal is to store image data in as little space as possible in a [[Computer file|file]]. Wavelet compression can be either [[lossless data compression|lossless]] or [[lossy data compression|lossy]].<ref>[[JPEG 2000]], for example, may use a 5/3 wavelet for lossless (reversible) transform and a 9/7 wavelet for lossy (irreversible) transform.</ref>

===Method===
First a wavelet transform is applied. This produces as many [[coefficient]]s as there are [[pixel]]s in the image (i.e., there is no compression yet since it is only a transform). These coefficients can then be compressed more easily because the information is statistically concentrated in just a few coefficients. This principle is called [[transform coding]]. After that, the coefficients are [[Quantization (signal processing)|quantized]] and the quantized values are [[entropy encoding|entropy encoded]] and/or [[run-length encoding|run length encoded]].

A few 1D and 2D applications of wavelet compression use a technique called "wavelet footprints".<ref>
 N. Malmurugan, A. Shanmugam, S. Jayaraman and V. V. Dinesh Chander.
 [http://www.acadjournal.com/2005/V14/part6/p1/ "A New and Novel Image Compression Algorithm Using Wavelet Footprints"]
</ref><ref>
 Ho Tatt Wei and Jeoti, V.
 "A wavelet footprints-based compression scheme for ECG signals".
 {{Cite book| doi = 10.1109/TENCON.2004.1414412| year = 2004| last1 = Ho Tatt Wei| volume = A| last2 = Jeoti | first2 = V.| pages = 283 | chapter = A wavelet footprints-based compression scheme for ECG signals| title = 2004 IEEE Region 10 Conference TENCON 2004| isbn = 0-7803-8560-8| s2cid = 43806122}}
</ref>

=== Evaluation ===

==== Requirement for image compression ====
For most natural images, the spectrum density of lower frequency is higher.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=J. Field|first=David|title=Relations between the statistics of natural images and the response properties of cortical cells|url=http://www.rctn.org/bruno/npb261b/field_87.pdf|journal=J. Opt. Soc. Am. A |volume=4 |pages=2379–2394 |year=1987|issue=12|doi=10.1364/JOSAA.4.002379|pmid=3430225|bibcode=1987JOSAA...4.2379F}}</ref> As a result, information of the low frequency signal (reference signal) is generally preserved, while the information in the detail signal is discarded. From the perspective of image compression and reconstruction, a wavelet should meet the following criteria while performing image compression:

* Being able to transform more original image into the reference signal.
* Highest fidelity reconstruction based on the reference signal.
* Should not lead to artifacts in the image reconstructed from the reference signal alone.

==== Requirement for shift variance and ringing behavior ====
Wavelet image compression system involves filters and decimation, so it can be described as a linear shift-variant system. A typical wavelet transformation diagram is displayed below:

[[File:Typical_wavelet_transform_diagram.png|border|frameless|510x510px]]

The transformation system contains two analysis filters (a low pass filter <math>h_0(n)</math> and a high pass filter <math>h_1(n)</math>), a decimation process, an interpolation process, and two synthesis filters (<math>g_0(n)</math> and <math>g_1(n)</math>). The compression and reconstruction system generally involves low frequency components, which is the analysis filters <math>h_0(n)</math> for image compression and the synthesis filters <math>g_0(n)</math> for reconstruction. To evaluate such system, we can input an impulse <math>\delta(n-n_i)</math> and observe its reconstruction <math>h(n-n_i)</math>; The optimal wavelet are those who bring minimum shift variance and sidelobe to <math>h(n-n_i)</math>. Even though wavelet with strict shift variance is not realistic, it is possible to select a wavelet with only slight shift variance. For example, we can compare the shift variance of two filters:<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Villasenor|first=John D.|title=Wavelet Filter Evaluation for Image Compression|journal=IEEE Transactions on Image Processing |volume=4 |issue=8 |date=August 1995|pages=1053–60|doi=10.1109/83.403412|pmid=18291999|bibcode=1995ITIP....4.1053V}}</ref>

By observing the impulse responses of the two filters, we can conclude that the second filter is less sensitive to the input location (i.e. it is less shift variant).

Another important issue for image compression and reconstruction is the system's oscillatory behavior, which might lead to severe undesired artifacts in the reconstructed image. To achieve this, the wavelet filters should have a large peak to sidelobe ratio.

So far we have discussed about one-dimension transformation of the image compression system. This issue can be extended to two dimension, while a more general term - shiftable multiscale transforms - is proposed.<ref>{{Cite journal|doi = 10.1109/18.119725|title = Shiftable multiscale transforms|year = 1992|last1 = Simoncelli|first1 = E.P.|last2 = Freeman|first2 = W.T.|last3 = Adelson|first3 = E.H.|last4 = Heeger|first4 = D.J.|journal = IEEE Transactions on Information Theory|volume = 38|issue = 2|pages = 587–607| s2cid=43701174 }}</ref>

==== Derivation of impulse response ====
As mentioned earlier, impulse response can be used to evaluate the image compression/reconstruction system.

For the input sequence <math>x(n)=\delta(n-n_i)</math>, the reference signal <math>r_1(n)</math> after one level of decomposition is <math>x(n)*h_0(n)</math> goes through decimation by a factor of two, while <math>h_0(n)</math> is a low pass filter. Similarly, the next reference signal <math>r_2(n)</math> is obtained by <math>r_1(n)*h_0(n)</math> goes through decimation by a factor of two. After L levels of decomposition (and decimation), the analysis response is obtained by retaining one out of every <math>2^L</math> samples: <math>h_A^{(L)}(n,n_i)=f_{h0}^{(L)}(n-n_i/2^L)</math>.

On the other hand, to reconstruct the signal x(n), we can consider a reference signal <math>r_L(n)=\delta(n-n_j)</math>. If the detail signals <math>d_i(n)</math> are equal to zero for <math>1\leq i \leq L</math>, then the reference signal at the previous stage (<math>L-1</math> stage) is <math>r_{L-1}(n)=g_0(n-2n_j)</math>, which is obtained by interpolating <math>r_L(n)</math> and convoluting with <math>g_0(n)</math>. Similarly, the procedure is iterated to obtain the reference signal <math>r(n)</math> at stage <math>L-2, L-3, ...., 1</math>. After L iterations, the synthesis impulse response is calculated: <math>h_s^{(L)}(n,n_i)=f_{g0}^{(L)}(n/2^L-n_j)</math>, which relates the reference signal <math>r_L(n)</math> and the reconstructed signal.

To obtain the overall L level analysis/synthesis system, the analysis and synthesis responses are combined as below:

<math>h_{AS}^{(L)}(n,n_i)=\sum_{k} f_{h0}^{(L)}(k-n_i/2^L)f_{g0}^{(L)}(n/2^L-k)</math>.

Finally, the peak to first sidelobe ratio and the average second sidelobe of the overall impulse response <math>h_{AS}^{(L)}(n,n_i)</math> can be used to evaluate the wavelet image compression performance.

Using a wavelet transform, the wavelet compression methods are adequate for representing [[Transient (acoustics)|transient]]s, such as percussion sounds in audio, or high-frequency components in two-dimensional images, for example an image of stars on a night sky. This means that the transient elements of a data signal can be represented by a smaller amount of information than would be the case if some other transform, such as the more widespread [[discrete cosine transform]], had been used.

=== Limitations ===

While wavelet transforms offer theoretical advantages, their practical limitations have effectively limited wavelet compression to analyzing localized changes and transient signals. Despite decades of research, wavelet-based compression systems for common multimedia like audio and video do not consistently match the efficiency and perceptual quality of current [[Discrete Cosine Transform]]-based systems.<ref name="x264dev"/>

For one-dimensional data like audio or ECGs, wavelets excel at representing and compressing transient signals—sudden, isolated events such as a drum hit in music or the sharp peaks in a heart rhythm. For example, the [[discrete wavelet transform]] has been successfully applied for the compression of electrocardiograph (ECG) signals.<ref>{{Cite journal|doi = 10.1109/10.649997|title = ECG coding by wavelet-based linear prediction|year = 1997|last1 = Ramakrishnan|first1 = A.G.|last2 = Saha|first2 = S.|journal = IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering|volume = 44|issue = 12|pages = 1253–1261|pmid = 9401225|s2cid = 8834327|url = http://eprints.iisc.ac.in/484/1/ECG_Coding_by_Wavelet-Based_Linear_Prediction.pdf}}</ref> However, for smooth, periodic signals, which make up much of typical audio, [[harmonic analysis]] in the [[frequency domain]] with [[List of Fourier-related transforms|Fourier-related transforms]] achieve better compression and [[sound quality]]. Compressing data that has both transient and periodic characteristics may be done with hybrid techniques that use wavelets along with traditional harmonic analysis. For example, the [[Vorbis]] [[audio codec]] primarily uses the [[modified discrete cosine transform]] to compress audio (which is generally smooth and periodic), however allows the addition of a hybrid wavelet [[filter bank]] for improved reproduction of transients.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2020-07-04 |title=Vorbis I specification |url=https://xiph.org/vorbis/doc/Vorbis_I_spec.html#x1-50001.1.2 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220403071601/http://xiph.org/vorbis/doc/Vorbis_I_spec.html#x1-50001.1.2 |archive-date=2022-04-03 |access-date=2022-04-10 |website=[[Xiph.Org Foundation]] |quote=Vorbis I is a forward-adaptive monolithic transform CODEC based on the Modified Discrete Cosine Transform. The codec is structured to allow addition of a hybrid wavelet filterbank in Vorbis II to offer better transient response and reproduction using a transform better suited to localized time events.}}</ref>

For higher-dimensional data, wavelet compression faces significant challenges. In video, for instance, modern compression techniques such as [[intra coding]] and [[motion compensation]] (predicting parts of an image based on what's next to it spatially and temporally) and mixed and dynamic block sizes become incredibly complex with wavelets because of their overlapping nature. This complexity translates to more processing power and slower speed, making them less practical for widespread use. Furthermore, while wavelets might score well on traditional measures such as [[PSNR]], DCT blocks create a perception of sharpness that wavelets often lack, requiring higher bitrates to achieve similar subjective quality.<ref name="x264dev">{{cite web |title=The problems with wavelets |url=http://x264dev.multimedia.cx/?p=317 |website=Diary Of An x264 Developer|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100228145846/http://x264dev.multimedia.cx/?p=317|archive-date=28 February 2010|url-status=dead|date=2 February 2010|first1=Jason|last1=Garrett-Glaser}}</ref>

==Comparison with Fourier transform and time-frequency analysis==
{| class="wikitable"
|-
! Transform !! Representation !! Input
|-
| [[Fourier transform]] || <math> \hat X(f) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(t)e^{-i2 \pi f t}\, dt</math>|| <math>f</math> : frequency
|-
| [[Time–frequency analysis]] || <math>X(t, f)</math> || <math> t </math> time; <math> f </math> frequency
|-
| Wavelet transform || <math> X(a,b) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{a}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\overline{\Psi\left(\frac{t - b}{a}\right)} x(t)\, dt </math> || <math> a </math> scaling ; <math> b </math> time shift factor
|}
Wavelets have some slight benefits over Fourier transforms in reducing computations when examining specific frequencies. However, they are rarely more sensitive, and indeed, the common [[Morlet wavelet]] is mathematically identical to a [[short-time Fourier transform]] using a Gaussian window function.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Bruns|first1=Andreas|title=Fourier-, Hilbert- and wavelet-based signal analysis: are they really different approaches?|journal=Journal of Neuroscience Methods|date=2004|volume=137|issue=2|pages=321–332|doi=10.1016/j.jneumeth.2004.03.002|pmid=15262077|s2cid=21880274}}</ref> The exception is when searching for signals of a known, non-sinusoidal shape (e.g., heartbeats); in that case, using matched wavelets can outperform standard STFT/Morlet analyses.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Krantz|first1=Steven G.|title=A Panorama of Harmonic Analysis|date=1999|publisher=Mathematical Association of America|isbn=0-88385-031-1}}</ref>

==Other practical applications==
The wavelet transform can provide us with the frequency of the signals and the time associated to those frequencies, making it very convenient for its application in numerous fields. For instance, signal processing of accelerations for gait analysis,<ref>{{Cite book | doi=10.1109/BIOWIRELESS.2011.5724356| chapter=Novel method for stride length estimation with body area network accelerometers| title=2011 IEEE Topical Conference on Biomedical Wireless Technologies, Networks, and Sensing Systems| pages=79–82| year=2011| last1=Martin| first1=E.| isbn=978-1-4244-8316-7| s2cid=37689047}}</ref> for fault detection,<ref>{{ cite journal | title=Shannon wavelet spectrum analysis on truncated vibration signals for machine incipient fault detection| journal=Measurement Science and Technology| year=2012 | last1=Liu | volume=23 | issue=5 | pages=1–11 | first1=Jie | doi=10.1088/0957-0233/23/5/055604| bibcode=2012MeScT..23e5604L| s2cid=121684952}}</ref> for the analysis of seasonal displacements of landslides,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Tomás |first1=R. |last2=Li |first2=Z. |last3=Lopez-Sanchez |first3=J. M. |last4=Liu |first4=P. |last5=Singleton |first5=A. |date=2016-06-01 |title=Using wavelet tools to analyse seasonal variations from InSAR time-series data: a case study of the Huangtupo landslide |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s10346-015-0589-y |journal=Landslides |language=en |volume=13 |issue=3 |pages=437–450 |doi=10.1007/s10346-015-0589-y |bibcode=2016Lands..13..437T |issn=1612-5118|hdl=10045/62160 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> for design of low power pacemakers and also in ultra-wideband (UWB) wireless communications.<ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1016/j.phycom.2009.07.001| title = Emerging applications of wavelets: A review| journal = Physical Communication| volume = 3| pages = 1–18| year = 2010| last1 = Akansu | first1 = A. N. | last2 = Serdijn | first2 = W. A. | last3 = Selesnick | first3 = I. W. | url = http://web.njit.edu/~akansu/PAPERS/ANA-IWS-WAS-ELSEVIER%20PHYSCOM%202010.pdf}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last1=Sheybani|first1=E.|last2=Javidi|first2=G.|title=2009 Second International Conference on Computer and Electrical Engineering |chapter=Dimensionality Reduction and Noise Removal in Wireless Sensor Network Datasets |date=December 2009|volume=2|pages=674–677|doi=10.1109/ICCEE.2009.282|isbn=978-1-4244-5365-8|s2cid=17066179}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last1=Sheybani|first1=E. O.|last2=Javidi|first2=G.|title=2012 International Conference on Systems and Informatics (ICSAI2012) |chapter=Multi-resolution filter banks for enhanced SAR imaging |date=May 2012|pages=2702–2706|doi=10.1109/ICSAI.2012.6223611|isbn=978-1-4673-0199-2|s2cid=16302915}}</ref>

{{ordered list|Discretizing of the <math>c-\tau</math> axis

Applied the following discretization of frequency and time:
:<math>\begin{align}
   c_n &= c_0^n \\
 \tau_m &= m \cdot T \cdot c_0^n
\end{align}</math>

Leading to wavelets of the form, the discrete formula for the basis wavelet:
:<math>\Psi(k, n, m) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{c_0^n}}\cdot\Psi\left[\frac{k - m c_0^n}{c_0^n}T\right] = \frac{1}{\sqrt{c_0^n}}\cdot\Psi\left[\left(\frac{k}{c_0^n} - m\right)T\right]</math>

Such discrete wavelets can be used for the transformation:
:<math>Y_{DW}(n, m) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{c_0^n}}\cdot\sum_{k=0}^{K - 1} y(k)\cdot\Psi\left[\left(\frac{k}{c_0^n} - m\right)T\right]</math>|Implementation via the FFT (fast Fourier transform)

As apparent from wavelet-transformation representation (shown below) 
:<math>Y_W(c, \tau) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{c}}\cdot\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} y(t) \cdot \Psi\left(\frac{t - \tau}{c}\right)\, dt </math>

where <math> c </math> is scaling factor, <math> \tau </math> represents time shift factor

and as already mentioned in this context, the wavelet-transformation corresponds to a [[convolution]] of a function <math>y(t) </math> and a wavelet-function. A convolution can be implemented as a multiplication in the frequency domain. With this the following approach of implementation results into:
* Fourier-transformation of signal <math>y(k) </math> with the FFT
* Selection of a discrete scaling factor <math>c_n</math>
* Scaling of the wavelet-basis-function by this factor <math>c_n</math> and subsequent FFT of this function
* Multiplication with the transformed signal YFFT of the first step
* Inverse transformation of the product into the time domain results in <math>Y_W(c, \tau)</math> for different discrete values of <math> \tau </math> and a discrete value of <math>c_n</math>
* Back to the second step, until all discrete scaling values for <math>c_n</math>are processed

There are many different types of wavelet transforms for specific purposes. See also a full [[list of wavelet-related transforms]] but the common ones are listed below: [[Mexican hat wavelet]], [[Haar Wavelet]], [[Daubechies wavelet]], triangular wavelet.|Fault detection in electrical power systems.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Silva |first1=K. M. |last2=Souza |first2=B. A. |last3=Brito |first3=N. S. D. |title=Fault detection and classification in transmission lines based on wavelet transform and ANN |journal=IEEE Transactions on Power Delivery |volume=21 |issue=4 |pages=2058–2063 |date=October 2006 |doi=10.1109/TPWRD.2006.876659|bibcode=2006ITPD...21.2058S |s2cid=36881450 }}</ref>|Locally adaptive statistical estimation of functions whose [[smoothness]] varies substantially over the domain, or more specifically, estimation of functions that are sparse in the wavelet domain.<ref>{{Cite book | last=Wasserman | first=L.A. | year=2005 | title=All of Nonparametric Statistics }}</ref>
}}

==Time-causal wavelets==

For processing temporal signals in real time, it is essential that the wavelet filters do not access signal values from the future as well as that minimal temporal latencies can be obtained. Time-causal wavelets representations have been developed by Szu et al<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1117/12.59911 | title=Causal analytical wavelet transform | year=1992 | last1=Szu | first1=Harold H. | last2=Telfer | first2=Brian A. | last3=Lohmann | first3=Adolf W. | journal=Optical Engineering | volume=31 | issue=9 | page=1825 | bibcode=1992OptEn..31.1825S }}</ref> and Lindeberg,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lindeberg |first1=T. |title=A time-causal and time-recursive scale-covariant scale-space representation of temporal signals and past time |journal=Biological Cybernetics |date=23 January 2023 |volume=117 |issue=1–2 |pages=21–59 |doi=10.1007/s00422-022-00953-6|pmid=36689001 |pmc=10160219 |doi-access=free }}</ref> with the latter method also involving a memory-efficient time-recursive implementation.

==Synchro-squeezed transform==
Synchro-squeezed transform can significantly enhance temporal and frequency resolution of time-frequency representation obtained using conventional wavelet transform.<ref>{{cite arXiv| last1 = Daubechies| first1 = Ingrid| last2 = Lu| first2 = Jianfeng| last3 = Wu| first3 = Hau-Tieng| title = Synchrosqueezed Wavelet Transforms: a Tool for Empirical Mode Decomposition| date = 2009-12-12| class = math.NA| eprint = 0912.2437}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal| doi = 10.1016/j.ymssp.2018.05.020| volume = 114| pages = 366–377| last1 = Qu| first1 = Hongya| last2 = Li| first2 = Tiantian| last3 = Chen| first3 = Genda| title = Synchro-squeezed adaptive wavelet transform with optimum parameters for arbitrary time series| journal = Mechanical Systems and Signal Processing| date = 2019-01-01| bibcode = 2019MSSP..114..366Q| s2cid = 126007150| doi-access = free}}</ref>
